title: Building on the Boundary: Roofs, Rainwater and Wastewater Next Door
desc: Building on the boundary without breaching neighbours' rights: roof rainwater, wastewater, windows, cutting walls and running cables across adjoining land.
summary: An owner's obligations when building on the boundary under the 2015 Civil Code: draining rainwater and wastewater, respecting shared walls, building rules, and rights to water supply, drainage and running lines across adjoining land.
body: p

Townhouses and tube houses are often built to fill the whole plot, hard against the neighbouring wall. Besides the construction permit, owners must comply with the obligations towards adjoining immovable property in the Civil Code 2015. Getting it right from the design stage avoids many conflicts with neighbours.
h2
1. The duty to respect building rules
p

Under Article 174, when building, the owner must comply with construction law, ensure safety, must not build beyond the height and distances that construction law sets, and must not infringe the lawful rights and interests of adjacent and surrounding house owners.
p

The space and ground beneath that may be used are measured in a vertical direction from the plot boundary (Clause 2, Article 175). So design roofs, overhangs and balconies so they do not project into the airspace above the neighbour's land without the neighbour's consent.
h2
2. Rainwater from the roof must not flow onto the neighbour
p
Under Article 250, the owner must install drainage channels so that rainwater from their roof or building does not flow onto the adjoining neighbour's land or house.
p
When designing a pitched roof on the boundary, slope the roof toward your own land, provide gutters and downpipes and lead the water into your own drainage system.
h2
3. Wastewater must have its own sewer or drain
p

Under Article 251, the owner must build an underground sewer or drainage ditch to take wastewater to the designated place, and not let it overflow onto the adjoining house, a public road or a public living area.
p

Conversely, if, because of natural position, water supply and drainage must pass across another person's land, that landowner must provide a suitable route for water supply and drainage and must not obstruct it; the person using this route must limit damage and pay compensation if damage is caused (Article 252).
h2
4. Windows, ventilation holes and shared walls
ul
For a shared house wall, you may not open windows or ventilation holes or cut into the wall to place structures if the neighbouring house does not consent (Clause 3, Article 176).
Where houses are built separately but the walls abut: each side may cut into the wall or place structures only up to the limit of its own wall.
Fences and dividing walls may be built only on your own land; to build on the boundary requires agreement (Clauses 1 and 2, Article 176).
p
To get light and ventilation for a house with walls abutting its neighbours, commonly used solutions are light wells, roof lights, or openings toward the front and rear facades on your own land.
h2
5. Running electric and communication lines across neighbouring land
p

An owner has the right to run power transmission and communication lines across other people's land in a reasonable way, ensuring safety and convenience for them; any damage caused must be compensated (Article 255). These rights are exercised by agreement; absent agreement, they must not be abused or made difficult for the other side (Article 248).
h2
6. Checklist when designing a house on the boundary
ol
Establish the boundary exactly, and do not let the roof, overhangs or balconies project into the neighbour's airspace.
Arrange gutters and rainwater and wastewater pipes entirely on your own land.
Do not open doors or ventilation holes in a shared wall; use a light well for daylight.
State clearly the measures to protect adjoining houses in the permit application and during construction – see Building causes a neighbour's house to settle or crack: liability and compensation.
Agree with the neighbour in writing on everything concerning the shared wall and drainage routes.
p

note

This article is only a summary for reference and does not replace the legal texts. Height, setbacks and the projection of balconies and overhangs are governed by planning and architecture standards and local regulations; check them when applying for a construction permit.
